notes: Take after completing the in-class git collaboration activity

questions.question: Before merging in Part 2, why do both partners `fetch` / check `git branch -r`?
options: To delete `main`
To confirm both feature branches exist on GitHub and that they still share the same `main`
To rewrite commit history
To create a pull request automatically
questions.explanation: Sync and verify catches missed pushes. Both should see `origin/feature-a` and `origin/feature-b` and the same `main` commit.

questions.question: Person A merges `feature-a` into `main` and Git just moves the `main` pointer forward. What is that called, and why?
options: A rebase, because commits were rewritten
A fast-forward, because `main` had not diverged from `feature-a` (it was still an ancestor)
A merge conflict, because two people edited the same file
A force push, because history changed on the remote
questions.explanation: When `main` is still an ancestor of the branch being merged, Git can fast-forward by sliding the pointer—no merge commit required.

questions.question: After Person A updates `main`, Person B's `feature-b` was created from an older `main`. What should Person B do before integrating?
options: Delete `feature-b` and start over on GitHub only
Update local `main` (`pull`), then bring that newest `main` into their feature work
Never touch `main` again
Run `git init` inside the feature branch
questions.explanation: Person B pulls the newest `main`, checks out `feature-b`, then merges (Part 2) or rebases (Part 3) so their branch includes Partner A's work.

questions.question: In Part 2, while on `feature-b`, Person B runs `git merge main` and gets conflict markers like `<<<<<<< HEAD`. What do those markers mean?
options: Git deleted both versions of the file
Git could not automatically combine overlapping edits; you must resolve them by hand
The repository is corrupted and must be re-cloned
SSH keys are missing
questions.explanation: Conflict markers show the two competing versions. Edit the file so both features work, remove the markers, then `git add` and finish the merge commit.

questions.question: After resolving a merge conflict on `feature-b`, what does the history typically include that a fast-forward would not?
options: A merge commit joining the divergent histories
No commits at all
Only Person A's commits
A deleted `main` branch
questions.explanation: Merging divergent branches creates a merge commit with two parents. That is different from a linear fast-forward.

questions.question: In Part 3, instead of `git merge main` on the feature branch, Person B runs `git rebase main`. What is the goal?
options: To delete Person A's commits from `main`
To replay the feature-branch commits on top of the newest `main` for a linear history
To convert the repo from git to SVN
To skip conflict resolution forever
questions.explanation: Rebase replays your unique commits onto the updated base. Conflicts can still happen, but the end history is a straight line instead of a merge commit.

questions.question: During `git rebase main`, which commits get rewritten (new hashes)?
options: Only commits that were unique to the feature branch being rebased
Every commit on `main`
All commits in the entire GitHub organization
None — rebase never changes hashes
questions.explanation: `main`'s commits stay as they are. Rebase copies/replays the feature commits as new commits on top of `main`.

questions.question: After a successful rebase of `rebase-b` onto `main`, merging `rebase-b` into `main` is often a fast-forward. Why?
options: Because rebase deletes `main`
Because `main` is once again an ancestor of the tip of `rebase-b`
Because GitHub ignores history
Because conflicts are impossible after a rebase
questions.explanation: Rebase put the feature commits directly ahead of `main`, so merging can just move the `main` pointer forward.

questions.question: Which statement best contrasts merge vs rebase for updating a feature branch with new `main` work?
options: Merge always rewrites history; rebase never creates commits
Merge can create a merge commit and preserve branch topology; rebase replays commits for a linear history (and rewrites those feature commits)
They are identical in every situation
Rebase only works on GitHub's website, not on the command line
questions.explanation: Both integrate changes and can involve conflicts. Merge keeps a join commit; rebase rewrites the feature commits into a linear sequence on top of `main`.

questions.question: Course practice in this activity says: do not develop directly on `main`. What should you do instead?
options: Commit only on `main` and never push
Create a feature branch for your work
Edit files only on GitHub's web UI
Disable `git status`
questions.explanation: Use feature branches (`feature-a`, `feature-b`, `rebase-a`, `rebase-b`, etc.), then integrate into `main` intentionally.
